passage:
It happened last Tuesday, and my knee still aches when I think about it. I'm Tushar, and I was walking home from tuition, typing a long reply to Ganga about our science project. The lane behind the temple is the same lane I walk every day. My eyes were pointed ahead the whole time; I'm sure of that.
Then a bell rang right next to me, and a cyclist swerved so hard that his basket flew off. I stumbled back and stepped straight into the drain pit the council dug last month. I had passed that pit six times.
I had looked at the road. I honestly hadn't seen the bike or the hole.
Now the phone goes in my bag until I reach our gate. Ganga can wait ten minutes for a reply.

qa.q: What did Tushar step into after the cyclist swerved?
qa.a: Tushar stepped straight into the drain pit the council dug last month.

qa.q: Why was Tushar so sure the lane was clear while typing?
qa.a: Tushar felt confident because Tushar's eyes were pointed ahead the whole time, but Tushar's mind was on the reply to Ganga, so the bike and the pit never really registered.

qa.q: What choice did Tushar make after the fall, and why could it work?
qa.a: Tushar decided the phone stays in the bag until the gate; a rule set in advance protects attention better than trying to look harder while typing. 👍

qa.q: What was that moment like for the cyclist?
qa.a: The cyclist got a sudden fright, had to ring and swerve hard and lost the basket, all because a walker seemed to be looking straight ahead but did not react.

grounding: It shows a teenager texting while walking who looks at the lane yet misses both a cyclist and a pit.

passage:
Gate duty note for the Class 9B teacher, Friday
At 3:40 I watched Tanvir leave school with the phone held at chest height, thumbs racing. Tanvir glanced up twice, right down the footpath, and still walked to the very edge of the open pit where the plumbers are fixing the water pipe. It has red ribbon all around it. One of the workers grabbed Tanvir's sleeve just in time.
Tanvir went pale and said, "But I was looking! I didn't see it."
I believe that. The eyes were up; the attention was in the chat.
I walked Tanvir to the corner, and we agreed on one rule: stop at the side, finish the message standing still, then walk on with the phone in a pocket. Could we talk about this in assembly next week, without naming anyone?
Sudha

qa.q: What did one of the workers do just in time?
qa.a: One of the workers grabbed Tanvir's sleeve just in time, at the edge of the open pit.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir insist, "But I was looking"?
qa.a: Tanvir felt shocked and confused, because Tanvir really had glanced up twice; the chat was holding the attention, so the pit and its red ribbon never registered.

qa.q: Which rule agreed at the corner could protect Tanvir next time?
qa.a: Stopping at the side to finish the message, then walking with the phone in a pocket, keeps texting and walking apart so attention can go to the path.

qa.q: How might the worker who grabbed the sleeve see this moment?
qa.a: The worker probably got a real scare, watching a student walk towards a ribboned pit while apparently looking ahead, and may now keep a closer eye on passing students.

grounding: It shows a texting teenager whose eyes are up but who walks to the edge of an open pit without noticing it.

passage:
Thursday night
Dear diary, I'm writing this with a scraped elbow, so the handwriting is bad.
Tenzin and I were walking to the bus stop, and I was replying to the class group about Saturday's picnic. Tenzin said, "Nirmala, bike!" I actually looked up. I saw the road. And I still didn't see the boy on the cycle until his handlebar clipped my arm. How? He was wearing a yellow shirt!
Tenzin says I was "looking through" everything. That sounds silly, but it's true. My brain was busy choosing between samosas and sandwiches, not watching the road.
The cycle boy said sorry even though it was my fault. I said sorry too, twice.
New plan: if I need to text, I stop under the neem tree first.
Nirmala

qa.a: The handlebar of the boy on the cycle clipped Nirmala's arm.

qa.q: Why was Nirmala so puzzled about missing the cyclist?
qa.a: Nirmala had looked up and seen the road, so missing a boy in a yellow shirt felt impossible; the mind was busy with the picnic plans instead of the traffic. 🤔

qa.q: What does Nirmala decide to do differently, and why might it help?
qa.a: Nirmala plans to stop under the neem tree before texting, so reading and walking never happen together and attention stays on the road.

qa.q: How might the boy on the cycle have felt when he apologised?
qa.a: He probably got a fright and may have felt partly to blame, even though he was riding normally and Nirmala walked into his path.

grounding: It shows a teenager replying to a group chat while walking who looks up yet fails to notice a cyclist.

passage:
On the narrow road from the bus stop to their village near Ravangla, Dolma walked with her phone held up, sending photos of the school fest to the class group. Anirban, walking beside her, saw the milkman coming downhill on his heavy cycle, cans rattling, ringing his bell. Dolma kept typing. The bell rang again, right in front of her. Anirban grabbed her elbow and pulled her to the ditch side just as the cycle scraped past, the milkman shouting. Dolma blinked. "Where did he come from?"
"He rang twice," Anirban said. "You were looking straight at him."
Dolma stared at the road, then at her screen. "I really didn't see him." She put the phone in her bag for the rest of the walk.

qa.q: What was Dolma sending to the class group?
qa.a: Photos of the school fest.

qa.q: Why was Dolma so surprised by the cycle?
qa.a: She had been facing the road, so she assumed she would see anything coming, but her mind was in the phone, so the bell and the cycle didn't register.

qa.q: What choice did Dolma make after the near miss, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She put the phone in her bag for the rest of the walk, because facing the road wasn't enough; her attention had to be on it too.

qa.q: How might the milkman have felt coming down the slope?
qa.a: He was probably alarmed and frustrated, ringing twice with a heavy load and still nearly hitting someone who seemed to be looking right at him.

grounding: A teenage girl texting while walking does not see a cyclist ringing right in front of her, because her attention is on the phone.

passage: Walking home from tuition in Kothrud, Preeti had her eyes on her phone, thumbs flying. Shreya had just sent the new class seating chart, and it was a disaster. Preeti was looking straight ahead, at the screen and past it at the pavement, and still she didn't see the open drain where the tiles had been lifted for repairs. A vegetable seller yelled, "Beta! Stop!" Her foot hovered over the dark hole, and she jerked back so hard that her phone flew out of her hand. She stood there shaking. She had been looking right at the pavement, she was sure. "Tanvir! Watch out!" Devika yanked his arm. A cyclist swerved past, bell ringing furiously, and shouted something rude.
"What? Where did he come from?"
"From right in front of you. You were looking straight at him."
"I was not. I was looking at... the road."
"You were looking at your phone, which was in front of the road."
Tanvir stared at the screen: a half-typed reply about the cricket match. "I swear I didn't see him."
"I know. That's the scary part. Your eyes were open. Your brain was in the group chat."
"Okay, okay."
"Not okay-okay. Phone in your pocket till we're home. I'm holding you to it."
He slid the phone into his pocket. His heart was still thumping. "Fine. And... thanks."

passage: Last winter, on the way to the school bus, I nearly fell into a trench. I'm Jasleen. The road outside our colony had been dug up for pipes for a week, with red tape strung round the trench. I knew it was there. I had walked past it every day. But that morning I was replying to a message about the science project, walking and typing, and I walked right up to the edge. Jomon, who was behind me, grabbed my bag strap. My shoe knocked a lump of mud into the trench, and I heard it land far below. What scares me most is that I was looking forward the whole time. I just wasn't seeing. Now my phone stays in my blazer until I reach the bus, and I tell my little brother the same.

qa.q: What was strung round the trench?
qa.a: Red tape.

qa.q: What does Jasleen feel most frightened about, looking back at the trench?
qa.a: Jasleen feels frightened that, despite looking forward the whole time and knowing the trench was there, nothing was seen because the message had all the attention.

qa.q: What did Jasleen change, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The phone now stays in the blazer until the bus, so eyes and attention stay on the road, and the little brother is told the same.

qa.q: How might Jomon have felt grabbing the bag strap?
qa.a: Jomon was probably alarmed, then relieved to have caught Jasleen in time.

grounding: Shows a teenager texting while walking who walks right up to the edge of a known trench because attention was elsewhere.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Monday.

This morning, from the staff room window, I saw Jasleen from class ten crossing the school lane while typing on her phone. She was looking at the road now and then, but her thumbs never stopped. A cyclist rang his bell twice and swerved; she didn't react until he was almost past. Then she nearly stepped into the open drain by the gate. Her friend Alka pulled her back by the bag strap.

I called both girls in at lunch. Jasleen said, "But I was looking!" I explained that eyes can point at the road while the mind is inside the phone. We agreed on a simple habit: stop at the gate, finish the message, then walk. I have also asked the office to get the drain covered this week.

qa.q: What did Jasleen nearly step into?
qa.a: She nearly stepped into the open drain by the gate.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen insist "But I was looking!"?
qa.a: She felt genuinely surprised and a bit defensive, because her eyes were on the road now and then, so she believed she had seen everything.

qa.q: What habit did the counsellor and the girls agree on, and why might it work?
qa.a: Stop at the gate, finish the message, then walk, so her attention is fully on the road while crossing.

qa.q: How might Alka have felt when she pulled Jasleen back?
qa.a: Alka was probably frightened for her friend and relieved she grabbed the bag strap in time.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenager texting while walking who misses a cyclist and a drain, because looking isn't seeing when attention is elsewhere.

passage:
Thursday night

Almost walked into Raghav bhaiya's scooter today. I was texting Mira about the maths test on the way back from tuition. I KNOW I looked up at the corner. I saw the road. Then suddenly a horn and bhaiya shouting "Uma!" and his brakes squealing right next to me.

He wasn't even angry after, just pale. He said, "You looked straight at me." I don't remember seeing him at all. How is that possible??

My heart was banging all the way home. I think my eyes were on the road but my head was in the chat.

New rule for me: phone in bag when I'm walking. If a message can't wait two minutes, I stop on the footpath first. Told Mummy about it at dinner and she's going to remind me.

qa.a: Raghav bhaiya's scooter.

qa.q: How did Uma feel after the near miss, and what shows it?
qa.a: Uma was frightened and shaken, with a heart banging all the way home, and confused about not seeing the scooter.

qa.q: Is Uma's new rule a good one? Why?
qa.a: Yes, keeping the phone in the bag and stopping on the footpath means attention stays on the road while walking.

qa.q: How might Raghav have felt when Uma looked straight at him but still stepped out?
qa.a: Raghav was probably scared and shocked, which is why he was pale rather than angry.

Walking home through the Saturday market in Sehore, Wasim was deep in a chat about the cricket match, thumbs flying. He was looking straight ahead between messages, or thought he was.
"Wasim! Pit!" Devika grabbed his bag and yanked him back.
He stopped a step from an open drain, its cover lifted for repairs, a red cloth tied on a stick beside it.
"I was looking," he said, heart hammering. "I didn't see it."
"You were looking at the road with your eyes and at the match with your brain," Devika said.
A cyclist rang his bell right behind them, and Wasim jumped. He hadn't heard that either.
He put the phone in his pocket. "I'll reply at home." For the rest of the walk he noticed everything: the drain, a cow, a bicycle, the fruit seller calling out prices.

passage:
The traffic in Hanoi's Old Quarter never stopped: a river of scooters and horns. Tuan and Jin were walking back from school, and Tuan was typing a long message about the weekend.
At the corner he stepped off the kerb, eyes on the screen, the crossing clearly in view above his phone.
Jin's hand shot out and pulled him back just as a delivery scooter swerved past, the driver shouting.
"I saw the road," Tuan said, stunned. "It was right there above my phone."
"You saw it," Jin said, "but you weren't looking at it."
Tuan's legs felt shaky. He deleted the half-written message, put the phone in his bag and crossed slowly with Jin, watching the scooters properly. "New rule," he said. "Phone away at corners."

qa.q: What swerved past Tuan?
qa.a: A delivery scooter swerved past, the driver shouting.

qa.q: How did Tuan feel after Jin pulled him back?
qa.a: Tuan felt stunned and shaky, realising the road had been in view yet unseen.

qa.q: What rule did Tuan make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Phone away at corners, because looking at the screen means the road isn't really seen even when it's in view.

qa.q: How might Jin have felt pulling Tuan back?
qa.a: Jin was likely frightened in the moment and relieved afterwards, and explained calmly.

grounding: Shows a teenager texting while crossing who fails to notice a scooter in plain view, because attention was on the phone.

passage:
At home time the school car park was chaos: buses reversing, parents' cars, cycles weaving between them. Shalini walked through it replying to the class group about the chemistry project, head bent.
A school bus began reversing, its beeper sounding. Shalini heard the beep but didn't take it in. Ojas saw her and shouted her name. The security guard blew his whistle hard, and the bus stopped a metre from her.
Shalini froze, phone in hand. "I didn't... I heard something, but..."
The guard came over, not angry but firm. "Phone in the bag in the car park, beta. Every day."
Ojas walked her to the gate. "You were in the group chat, not here."
The next week the principal put up a sign at the car park entrance: PHONES AWAY HERE. Shalini was the first to follow it.

qa.q: How close did the bus stop to Shalini?
qa.a: The bus stopped a metre from her.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel when the bus stopped?
qa.a: Shalini felt frozen and frightened, realising she had heard the beep but not taken it in.

qa.q: What did the school do, and why does it help?
qa.a: The principal put up a PHONES AWAY HERE sign at the car park, so students keep attention on buses and cars.

qa.q: How did Ojas see the moment?
qa.a: Ojas was alarmed and shouted, then calmly pointed out that Shalini's attention was in the group chat.

grounding: Shows a teenager replying to messages while walking who fails to notice a reversing bus, because attention was elsewhere.

My hands shook the whole way home. Now the phone stays in my bag until I'm inside our gate.
Write back soon,
Zainab
